explanation: Mockito records matchers on a stack as they are evaluated. A raw value leaves no matcher on the stack, so Mockito cannot align arguments to matchers and throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException. The fix is to wrap every argument in a matcher, e.g. when(repo.find(anyString(), eq(10))). The other options describe behaviour Mockito does not have.
options: Mockito treats the raw value as eq() automatically and the stub works.
Mockito throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException at runtime.
The stub compiles but is silently ignored.
Mockito matches only the first argument and ignores the second.
prompt: What happens when you mix a raw value and an argument matcher in a single Mockito stubbing call, such as when(repo.find(anyString(), 10))?
title: Mixing matchers and raw values

explanation: Cost and speed increase up the pyramid while failure precision decreases, so most coverage belongs in cheap, precise unit tests, with fewer integration tests for wiring and a few end-to-end tests for critical journeys. A suite dominated by end-to-end tests is the slow, hard-to-debug ice-cream cone anti-pattern.
options: Mostly end-to-end tests, with a few unit tests at the top.
Equal numbers of unit, integration, and end-to-end tests.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few end-to-end tests.
Only unit tests, because integration tests are never worth their cost.
prompt: Which shape describes a healthy test suite according to the test pyramid?
title: Test pyramid shape

explanation: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer, which is exactly what mapping and validation need, and @MockitoBean replaces the service. @SpringBootTest would work but is far slower than necessary, a plain unit test would not exercise Spring MVC mapping or validation, and @DataJpaTest loads the wrong layer entirely.
options: @SpringBootTest with a real server, because it is the most faithful option.
A plain unit test calling the controller method directly, because no context is ever needed.
@WebMvcTest with the service replaced by @MockitoBean, tested through MockMvc.
@DataJpaTest, because it loads the persistence layer the controller needs.
prompt: A controller test needs to verify request mapping and validation, but the service layer is not under test. Which is the best choice?
title: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest

explanation: Docker maps the container's internal port (5432) to a random free host port, so the service is reachable on the host only through that mapped port, reported by getMappedPort(5432) or wired automatically by @ServiceConnection. Connecting to 5432 on the host only works by coincidence, and Testcontainers does not edit application.properties.
options: Always use 5432, the standard PostgreSQL port.
Use the mapped port reported by the container, e.g. container.getMappedPort(5432).
Use the port from application.properties, because Testcontainers updates that file.
Use any free port, because Testcontainers forwards all ports automatically.
prompt: A Testcontainers PostgreSQL container is running. How should test code obtain the port to connect to?
title: Testcontainers mapped ports

back: A mock is a Mockito object with no real behaviour, used for stubbing answers and verifying calls. A fake is a small real implementation, such as an in-memory repository backed by a HashMap, with genuine behaviour.
front: What is the difference between a mock and a fake in testing?
title: Mock vs fake

back: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating (it passes or fails on its own), and Timely (written close to the code it covers).
front: What does FIRST stand for as qualities of a good test?
title: FIRST test qualities

back: @MockitoBean (Spring Boot 3.4+, replacing the deprecated @MockBean) replaces a bean in a Spring test context with a Mockito mock. It must not be used in a plain unit test, where there is no context; use @Mock there.
front: What is @MockitoBean, and where must it not be used?
title: @MockitoBean

description: Write a JUnit 5 + Mockito unit test for DiscountService (constructor takes a PriceRepository with double findPrice(String productCode); discountedPrice(productCode, percent) throws IllegalArgumentException for percent outside 0-100). Cover: a 10% discount on a price of 100.0 returns 90.0, and a percent of 150 throws IllegalArgumentException. Use @Mock and @InjectMocks with MockitoExtension.
hints: Use assertThrows for the invalid-percent case and check the result with assertEquals and a delta.
title: Write a unit test for a discount service

description: SubscriptionService takes a java.time.Clock in its constructor and has boolean isExpired(LocalDate expiryDate), which returns true when the current date (from the clock) is after the expiry date. Write a test that freezes time at 2026-11-04 (UTC) and asserts that an expiry date of 2026-11-04 is not expired while 2026-11-03 is expired.
hints: Pass the fixed clock into the SubscriptionService constructor.
This makes the test repeatable on any date, instead of depending on LocalDate.now().

description: HelloController has GET /hello with a required request parameter 'name', delegating to GreetingService.greet(name). Write a @WebMvcTest slice test that: (1) stubs greet("Beanstack") to "Hello, Beanstack" and asserts a 200 response with that body, and (2) asserts that a request with no name parameter returns 400. Use @MockitoBean for the service.
hints: Annotate the class with @WebMvcTest(HelloController.class) and autowire MockMvc.
Use mockMvc.perform(get("/hello").param("name", "Beanstack")) with status() and content() matchers.

explanation: Unstubbed Mockito methods return default values: 0 for numeric primitives such as double, false for boolean, null for objects, and empty collections for collection return types. findPrice returns double, so both calls print 0.0. Mockito does not require stubbing before use and does not throw for unstubbed calls.
options: 100.0, then an exception
null, null
It does not compile, because unstubbed mocks must be stubbed first
prompt: What does this code print? The mock is a plain Mockito mock with no stubbing.
title: Unstubbed mock return values

explanation: verify(mock).method() defaults to times(1), exactly one invocation. Two calls fail verification; the test would need verify(priceRepository, times(2)).findPrice("BOOK") to pass. Verification works fine after stubbed calls, and it counts invocations, not distinct arguments.
options: It passes, because verify defaults to at least once.
It fails, because verify defaults to exactly once and the method was called twice.
It passes, because verification counts distinct arguments, not calls.
It fails, because verify cannot be used after a stubbed call.
prompt: A test calls discountService.discountedPrice("BOOK", 20) twice, with the repository stubbed, and then runs the verification shown. What happens?
title: Verify times count

description: A test suite passes when tests are run individually but sometimes fails when the whole suite runs. One failing test reads the current date, another writes to a shared static map that a later test reads, and a third waits for an async job with Thread.sleep(200). Diagnose each failure source and propose a concrete fix for each, plus the process for handling the flaky tests in the meantime.
solution: All three are classic flakiness sources. (1) The date-dependent test should inject a java.time.Clock and use Clock.fixed in tests, so 'now' is controlled and repeatable. (2) The shared static map is shared mutable state: reset it in @BeforeEach (or remove the static sharing) so no test depends on execution order or another test's leftovers. (3) The Thread.sleep guess should be replaced by awaiting a condition with a timeout (e.g. Awaitility), so the test waits exactly until the async work completes. Process: quarantine the flaky tests so their failures do not block the suite, reproduce each (run the suite repeatedly), fix the root cause, and only then un-quarantine. Do not just delete them, which would silently lose coverage.
title: Diagnosing a flaky test suite

description: A repository test suite passes against the default embedded database in @DataJpaTest, but the same queries fail in production on PostgreSQL. Explain the likely cause, how to reproduce the failure in tests, and what changes to make to the test setup.
solution: The likely cause is a dialect difference: H2 tolerates SQL, types, or functions that PostgreSQL rejects (or vice versa), so the embedded database hides a real failure. Reproduce it by running the repository tests against real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers: add a static @Container PostgreSQLContainer with @ServiceConnection, annotate the test with @Testcontainers, and set @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) on the @DataJpaTest so the container database is actually used instead of being silently replaced by H2. Pin the image tag to a major version (e.g. postgres:16). Keep these container tests focused on database-specific behaviour; the rest of the suite stays at cheaper layers.
title: Tests pass on H2 but fail on PostgreSQL
